description: We are aiming to build the best health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions.
summary:
Far from Earth, there’s no doctor down the hall. On long missions, astronauts have to check their own health and decide when something needs attention, often with slow or no contact with the ground. We built Vital Sync to help with that.

Sharan and Vedanti, from Team V-Sync sat down to ideate for this problem, and that's how Vital Sync was born. Vital Sync is a web app that walks a crew member through a daily health check, one step at a time. Every step is read aloud and has an illustrated guide, and readings can be spoken instead of typed. It covers 25 checks: daily vitals, weekly wellbeing using validated scales like the PSS-4, periodic tests such as hydration and ultrasound with camera colour matching, and cabin readings like CO₂ and radiation.

The app then turns those numbers into plain answers. Each body system gets a clear status linked to NASA’s known spaceflight health risks, a 3D body view shows where to look, and a spoken flight-surgeon-style debrief explains what to do next. Streaks and badges help the routine stick.

It runs offline in a browser with nothing to install and adapts from the ISS to a pressurized lunar rover. As crews head to the Moon and Mars, that independence will matter more and more.
details:
GitHub: https://github.com/tsharan17/Vital-Sync
Live app: https://vitalsync-vsync.vercel.app

Built by Sharan and Vedanti, Team V-Sync.

What does it do or how does it work?

On the ISS, an astronaut who feels unwell can talk to a flight surgeon on the ground within minutes. On the way to Mars, a message can take up to forty minutes for the round trip, and sometimes there’s no link at all. We wanted to give the crew a tool that walks them through their own health check and tells them, in plain words, what the results mean and what to do about them. That’s Vital Sync.

The app always opens on a clearance screen, because the tests come before anything else. From there it guides the astronaut through the check-in one step at a time. Every step is read aloud with pause, play and repeat controls, and each test has a small, illustrated guide showing how to do it. Readings can be spoken instead of typed: say “one eighteen over seventy six” and the app turns that into a blood pressure entry.

There are 25 checks, grouped by how often they’re needed:

  • Every day: vitals, sleep, mood, a cognitive test and a breathing count. The breathing count starts with a 32-second paced breathing warm-up, then counts breaths for a full minute without pacing, so the number isn’t skewed.
  • Every week: the PSS-4 stress scale and the Three-Item Loneliness Scale. Both are published, validated questionnaires, so we didn’t have to invent our own questions.
  • Periodic: tests like hydration and ultrasound. For hydration, the astronaut points the camera at a sample and the app matches the colour against a standard hydration chart.
  • Automatic: cabin readings like CO₂ and radiation dose sit alongside the body data.

The cognitive test is a reaction-time task, similar to the psychomotor vigilance test used in spaceflight research to spot fatigue. Once everything is in, the app gives each body system a status and links it to the human spaceflight risks NASA tracks. A 3D body lets you tap any region to see its status and related risks. A flight-surgeon-style voice then gives a short debrief of how you’re doing today and what to do next. When there’s a link to Earth, the crew can send a short report to the ground team or have it read aloud.

The app also knows where the crew is. In a pressurized lunar rover, space is tighter, CO₂ builds up faster and checks are needed more often than on the ISS, so the rules change to match.

What benefits does it have?

Most health tools for astronauts assume someone on the ground will read the data and make the call. Vital Sync turns that around. It is the crew’s own health officer: it collects the readings, makes sense of them and explains what to do, all on the device and with no signal needed.

What makes this possible is the combination, not any one feature on its own:

  • Fully guided, voice-first checks. Every step is read aloud and readings can be spoken back. A tired astronaut, or one with gloves on or hands full, can get through the whole routine almost entirely by listening and talking. On a mission where every minute of crew time is planned, a check that runs itself is a real saving.
  • Answers, not just numbers. The app links each result to the spaceflight health risks NASA tracks. It shows where the problem is on a 3D body and gives a spoken, flight-surgeon-style debrief. The crew doesn’t need medical training to understand where they stand.
  • Ordinary hardware, new uses. A regular tablet camera becomes a hydration test reader through colour matching, and the microphone replaces the keyboard. Nothing extra has to be launched.
  • Mind as well as body. Weekly stress and loneliness checks use validated scales, so slow problems like isolation or burnout show up as trends before they affect the mission.
  • Built to adapt. The rules change with the environment, from the ISS to a cramped lunar rover.
  • Private by design. Health data never leaves the device unless the crew chooses to send it.
  • A habit people keep. Streaks, badges, a daily quest and an EVA clearance stamp turn a chore into a mission. A monitoring tool only works if it gets used every day.

What is the intended impact of the project?

On the way to Mars, help from Earth stops being instant. Crews will need to catch and handle health problems on their own, and the tools they rely on today aren’t built for that. We see Vital Sync as a step toward real crew medical independence: a routine that spots problems early, guides the next step clearly, and hands the flight surgeon clean, consistent data whenever contact comes back.

Because it runs in any browser, offline and with no special hardware, the same approach can reach people on Earth who live far from a doctor. That includes researchers at polar stations, crews at sea and patients in rural communities. A system built to keep astronauts safe millions of kilometres from help can do the same for people a few hundred kilometres from the nearest clinic.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Language and build. The app is plain JavaScript using ES modules, built with Vite 5. We skipped a heavy framework on purpose so it loads fast and runs well on modest devices. Navigation uses simple hash-based routing, so the whole app is static files and needs no server.
  • Architecture. The health logic sits in its own pure engine, completely separate from the interface, so the logic can be tested on its own. That includes scoring, thresholds, scales, streaks, the debrief and the environment rules. Node’s built-in test runner checks it with 25 automated tests.
  • Validated scales. The PSS-4 is scored with two items reverse-scored, giving a 0–16 range. The loneliness scale gives a 3–9 range. Both are converted into a simple 1–5 level for the dashboard, and the app keeps track of when each weekly check is due.
  • Voice. We use the browser’s Web Speech API: speech synthesis to read every step aloud, and speech recognition for voice entry. One shared player controls all narration in the app, which is what gives the pause, play, back, next and repeat controls. It ignores out-of-date callbacks, so two voices never talk over each other. We also wrote our own parser that turns spoken phrases like “one eighteen over seventy six” into numbers.
  • Camera. The app asks for the camera through the browser, and falls back to a normal photo upload on devices that don’t allow live access. Each photo is shrunk to a maximum of 480 pixels and compressed before saving. For hydration, the app averages the colour in the centre of the image and finds the closest match on the hydration chart.
  • 3D. The interactive body is built with three.js.
  • Sound. Small sound effects, like clicks, chimes and the EVA stamp, use the Web Audio API, with a volume control.
  • Themes. Light and “Satellite” dark themes are built with CSS variables, and even the illustrations use them, so they recolour automatically. A small script applies the theme before the page draws, so it never flashes the wrong colours.
  • Storage. All data is saved in the browser’s local storage on the device. The app watches the storage limit and warns the user instead of silently losing data.
  • Illustrations. We generated the illustrated test guides as SVG files using a Python script.
  • Version control and hosting. The code is on GitHub and hosted on Vercel, which redeploys automatically on every update.
  • Demo video. We recorded and edited it with Playwright, FFmpeg and Python, and used public-domain NASA footage.

Hardware: nothing special. Any phone, tablet or laptop with a modern browser works. The camera and microphone are optional extras.

How is your project creative?

Health checklists are boring, and boring things get skipped. So, we built Vital Sync to feel like a game mission:

  • a side menu styled like a game HUD with a daily quest
  • illustrated mission cards
  • streak rewards at 3, 7, 14, 30, 60 and 100 days, and holographic badges
  • a “cleared for EVA” stamp as a final self-check before a spacewalk

Voice isn’t tucked away in a separate audio tab; it runs through every single screen, so you can use the whole app mostly by listening and speaking. The camera colour matching turns an ordinary tablet into a simple test reader. The 3D body turns a list of numbers into something you can see and touch.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Distance from Earth. The app works with no connection and nothing to install.
  • Crew time and fatigue. Steps are short, read aloud and accept voice input.
  • Credibility. We used validated questionnaires and linked results to NASA’s documented spaceflight risks instead of making up our own categories.
  • Safety. Vital Sync supports decisions. It doesn’t diagnose, and it doesn’t replace the flight surgeon.
  • Privacy. Data stays on the device unless the crew chooses to send a report.
  • Different environments. The rules change between the ISS and a lunar rover.
  • Accessibility. Clear contrast, two themes, keyboard support and audio on every screen.
  • Limited resources. Photos are compressed and storage is monitored, so the app stays small and reliable.
